title: Hurricane Rachel (September–October 2026): a long-lived hurricane and a deadly remnant
description: Research paper on Hurricane Rachel, eastern Pacific, September–October 2026.
obs_cutoff: IBTrACS to 11 Oct; NHC discussions 1–58; press to 16 Oct
status_note: Draft for review (24 Oct 2026). Built from provisional data; to be checked against NHC's Tropical Cyclone Report when published.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.html: Rachel was a long-lived eastern Pacific hurricane whose most damaging effects came after it had stopped being a hurricane. It formed south of Mexico on 27 September, strengthened slowly through days of 15–20 kt northeasterly shear, intensified rapidly by 30 kt in 24 hours near Socorro Island and peaked at 105 kt (120 mph, Category 3) and 950 mb at 2 Oct 0000 UTC. It then remained a hurricane for six more days while drifting west over water that was unusually warm for the latitude (about 26 °C, +1.5 °C against normal), before a deep trough swept it northeast. As a post-tropical cyclone it crossed northern Baja California near Ensenada early on 11 October with winds near 50 kt and dissipated over the southwestern United States the same day. Flooding in the municipality of Ensenada killed eight people, and Rachel's waves, combined with a long-period swell, spring tides and sea levels already raised by El Niño, caused coastal flooding and erosion in Southern California.

sections.title: Main findings
sections.html:
1. Strengthening against shear. For four days Rachel's centre lay at the northern edge of its convection under about 20 kt of northeasterly shear NHC discussion 6, NHC discussion 10, yet it became a hurricane at 30 Sep 0600 UTC and then rapidly intensified, from 75 kt to 105 kt in 24 hours.
  2. Long hurricane life. Rachel spent 192 hours as a hurricane and produced 26.9 × 10⁴ kt² of ACE, as much as Simon. Repeated dry-air intrusions caused fluctuations but not collapse NHC discussion 32, NHC discussion 38.
  3. A strong cold wake. Moving slowly, Rachel cooled the sea under its track by up to 2.8 °C in the analysis, near 19.4°N, 110.2°W on 2 Oct 0600 UTC.
  4. Deadliest as a remnant. All eight deaths occurred in Ensenada, Baja California, after Rachel had become post-tropical; four of the dead were children.
  5. Compound coastal hazard. In Southern California, waves from Rachel met a long-period southerly swell and water levels running up to 1.5 ft above predictions.

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.html: Rachel was the eighteenth tropical cyclone of the 2026 eastern North Pacific season and the second of four major hurricanes off southwestern Mexico between 22 September and 16 October. Its track, first parallel to Mexico and then west and northeast towards Baja California, linked the hyperactive tropical season to the coastal ocean off California, where El Niño had already raised sea level [12]. This paper reconstructs Rachel's life cycle and the chain of events that turned a weakening storm into a deadly one.

sections.title: 2. Data and methods
sections.html:
Track and intensity. Six-hourly positions, 1-minute maximum sustained winds and minimum pressures from IBTrACS v04r01 [1], downloaded on 24 October 2026. For 2026 these are provisional values carried over from the operational advisories (National Hurricane Center); the official best track, issued in the post-season report, can differ. Rapid intensification (RI) is an increase of at least 30 kt in 24 hours [2]. Accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) sums the squared 6-hourly winds at tropical-storm strength or above.

Ocean. Sea-surface temperature (SST) and its anomaly against 1991–2020 from NOAA OISST v2.1 daily [3], sampled at each 6-hourly position three days before the storm arrived, so that the storm's own cooling is excluded; the change from three days before to three days after gives the cold wake. OISST is a 0.25° analysis and smooths very small wakes.

Atmosphere. Wind shear and mid-level humidity are taken from the forecasters' own analyses in the advisories and discussions (which use the SHIPS model and satellite estimates), quoted with date and time. Our planned reanalysis diagnostics could not be computed because the NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 daily files for 2026 end on 17 March 2026. The Madden–Julian oscillation (MJO) is described by the real-time RMM index [4] (phase and amplitude; amplitude ≥ 1 means an active MJO). ENSO values are NOAA CPC indices (RONI JAS 2026 +1.69 °C; weekly relative Niño 3.4 +2.4 °C in mid-October).

Impacts. Deaths, damage and observations are taken from official statements where available and otherwise from wire-service reports, each cited; figures are preliminary.

sections.title: 3. Life cycle
sections.html:
Genesis and a sheared start (25–30 September). IBTrACS follows the precursor from 25 Sep 0000 UTC near 9.2°N, 92.6°W. The depression formed early on 27 September; SHIPS guidance suggested shear would limit development at first NHC discussion 1. For the next three days Rachel endured about 20 kt of northeasterly shear, with its low-level centre near the northern edge of the convection NHC discussion 4, NHC discussion 6, NHC discussion 10. It strengthened anyway, helped by bursts of very deep convection with cloud tops near −90 °C NHC discussion 10. On 29 September a NOAA P-3 research flight, with an uncrewed aircraft launched into the storm, measured 66 kt at 700 mb NHC discussion 11.

Peak near Socorro Island (30 September – 2 October). Rachel became a hurricane at 30 Sep 0600 UTC. As the shear relaxed it intensified from 75 kt to 105 kt between 0000 UTC on 1 and 2 October, with a ragged eye inside cloud tops near −85 °C NHC discussion 20, and passed closest to Socorro Island on 2 October NHC discussion 22. Dry air already affected a loose eyewall NHC discussion 22.

Six days as a weakening hurricane (2–8 October). A ridge to the north steered Rachel slowly west NHC discussion 26, NHC discussion 30. Its eye cleared and filled several times as northeasterly shear brought dry air into the northern side NHC discussion 32, NHC discussion 34, NHC discussion 38, NHC discussion 42. Winds varied between 65 and 90 kt; Rachel fell below hurricane strength only on 8–9 October.

Recurvature and post-tropical transition (8–11 October). A deep mid- to upper-level trough approaching the west coast of the United States slowed Rachel, then turned it northeast and accelerated it NHC discussion 44, NHC discussion 48, NHC discussion 49. Under 25–35 kt of southwesterly shear its convection became shallow and frontal in structure NHC discussion 54, and at 0300 UTC on 11 October it was declared post-tropical NHC discussion 56. Its winds increased again to 50–55 kt through baroclinic interaction with the trough. The centre crossed northern Baja California near 31.8°N, 116.3°W around 0600 UTC on 11 October and the system dissipated over the southwestern United States NHC discussion 58.

sections.title: 4. Environment
sections.html:
Ocean. Up to the peak the sea ahead of Rachel averaged 29.6 °C, +1.1 °C above normal. During its long westward drift on 6–9 October the water was about 25.8 °C, cooler but still +1.5 °C above normal for the season and latitude, part of the warm anomaly off Baja California. Near Baja California on 11 October the sea was 25.5 °C, +4.9 °C above normal: too cool to sustain a hurricane, but an exceptional marine heatwave. Rachel's slow motion produced the strongest cold wake of the storms in this batch: up to 2.8 °C [5]. The wake it left near 14°N, 102°W on 29 September was still visible two weeks later under Trudy (see the Trudy paper).

Shear and moisture. Northeasterly shear of 15–20 kt persisted from 27 September to 30 September NHC discussion 6, NHC discussion 14; dry air intruded repeatedly after the peak NHC discussion 26, NHC discussion 32, NHC discussion 34; strong southwesterly shear accompanied the transition NHC discussion 54.

MJO. RMM phase 2 (amplitude 0.9) at genesis and phase 2 (1.2) during rapid intensification [6]; not tested further.

sections.title: 5. Impacts
sections.html:
Baja California. Heavy rain from Rachel's remnant caused flooding and landslides in the municipality of Ensenada over the weekend of 10–11 October and knocked out power; a stream in the Buena Vista community overflowed, sweeping away vehicles, animals and a cabin [10]. By 15 October the death toll was eight, all in Ensenada, four of them minors, with two people still missing [11]. Soldiers rescued 32 people, including 13 children, by helicopter from an orphan camp near Ensenada; a father and son fishing from San Felipe on the Gulf of California were missing [10].

Southern California. The hurricane centre warned that waves from Rachel, combined with an incoming long-period southerly swell, would produce life-threatening surf and rip currents, and that major coastal flooding was already occurring, with water levels running up to 1.5 ft above predictions; flooding and erosion were expected to worsen as the highest waves coincided with high tides NHC discussion 54. The elevated water levels reflect El Niño's coastally trapped wave and the warm ocean along the coast [12]. The remnant then brought a risk of flash flooding to the southwestern United States NHC discussion 58.

sections.title: 6. Climate context
sections.html: Rachel's long life at 20°N and its deadly remnant both depended on an ocean that was much warmer than usual off western Mexico and Baja California, during a very strong El Niño [8] and an exceptionally active season [7]. The Southern California coastal flooding was a compound event: storm waves, a distant swell, spring tides and a sea level raised by El Niño. No attribution study exists.

sections.title: 7. Uncertainties
sections.html:
• Provisional track and intensities; the post-tropical crossing point and time are approximate.
  • The deaths were caused by flash flooding from the remnant; rainfall totals were not available.
  • The size of Rachel's contribution to the Southern California coastal flooding, relative to the swell, tides and El Niño sea level, was not quantified.

sections.title: 8. Conclusion
sections.html: Rachel strengthened despite persistent shear, peaked briefly as a major hurricane over open water and lingered as a hurricane for almost a week over an ocean warmed by El Niño. Its greatest harm came later, as a fast-moving post-tropical cyclone whose rain flooded Ensenada and whose waves reached a Southern California coast already running high. The case shows why post-tropical remnants deserve the same attention as the hurricane itself.
